summary: Gives operators recommendations for running Segment Routing LSPs alongside RSVP-TE LSPs in the same network, including while services migrate from one to the other. It discusses how the two can coexist, including sharing links and bandwidth, and what to watch out for during the transition.

plainLanguage.summary: A town is adding a new bus system while the old one still runs. This explains how both can share the same roads without crashing into each other.

questions: migrate from rsvp-te to segment routing
how to migrate from rsvp-te to segment routing
subtitle: Running two advanced routing protocols safely in the same network during transition

tldr.problem: Network operators introducing Segment Routing (SR) LSPs to networks already running RSVP-TE LSPs face a problem: the two protocols don't see each other's traffic, so the bandwidth available for RSVP-TE paths is incorrectly calculated and traffic may be misrouted or dropped.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes five solution options for coexistence, from static bandwidth partitioning to dynamic measurement of SR traffic and reduction of available bandwidth for RSVP-TE. The preferred option measures SR utilization and adjusts RSVP-TE limits dynamically.
tldr.outcome: Operators can safely migrate from RSVP-TE to Segment Routing without a flag-day cutover, managing bandwidth correctly throughout the transition.

today: RFC 8426 is an Informational RFC published in July 2018 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the authoritative guide for operators transitioning networks from RSVP-TE to Segment Routing.

sections.title: The Coexistence Problem
sections.content:
RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol with Traffic Engineering) is the established way for networks to reserve bandwidth on specific paths. Segment Routing (SR) is a newer approach that simplifies traffic engineering by encoding path information in packet headers instead of using reserved connections.

When operators introduce SR to networks already running RSVP-TE, a key problem emerges: RSVP-TE calculates available bandwidth based on link capacity minus RSVP-TE reservations. It does not see SR traffic, so it incorrectly believes more bandwidth is available than there actually is. This can cause RSVP-TE to place traffic on overloaded links or fail to reserve paths it should accept. The RFC calls this the "dark bandwidth" problem.
sections.plainLanguage: The new bus system doesn't tell the old system how many passengers it's carrying. So the old system thinks the road is more empty than it really is and sends too many buses there.

sections.title: Design Constraints
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five key requirements for a coexistence solution. First, the solution must keep the Traffic Engineering Database (TED) consistent across the network. Second, RSVP-TE path computers may have no knowledge of SR. Third, existing RSVP-TE path computation logic should not require changes or software upgrades. Fourth, new protocol extensions should be minimal because coexistence may only be temporary. Fifth, RSVP-TE paths in distributed networks should not require migration to a central controller.

These constraints make the problem challenging: the solution must work with existing RSVP-TE equipment and practices while accounting for SR traffic transparently.
sections.plainLanguage: The fix must work with the old system as-is, not break how it calculates routes, and not force everything to be controlled from one place.

sections.title: Five Solution Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC describes five options. Static bandwidth partitioning reserves a fixed amount of bandwidth for SR and the rest for RSVP-TE; this is simple but wastes bandwidth when one protocol is idle. Centralized management uses a single controller to place both types of paths and track bandwidth; this requires deploying a new controller, which is not practical for existing networks.

Flooding SR utilization in IGP spreads SR traffic information through the routing protocol so RSVP-TE path computers can see it; this requires upgrading path computation logic in many places. Running SR over RSVP-TE places SR traffic inside dedicated RSVP-TE paths; this lets the TED stay consistent but makes SR depend on RSVP-TE.

The preferred option, TED consistency by reflecting SR traffic, dynamically measures SR traffic on each link and reduces the bandwidth advertised as available for RSVP-TE. This approach requires no protocol changes and no upgrades to RSVP-TE path computers.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1: Give the old system 60% of the road, the new system 40%. Option 2: One control room decides everything. Option 3: Tell routers about new buses. Option 4: New buses go inside old reserved lanes. Option 5: Measure new buses and tell the old system the road is actually fuller than it looks.

sections.title: Dynamic Traffic Measurement
sections.content:
The preferred option works by collecting SR traffic statistics at intervals and calculating averages over time. When the average changes significantly (beyond a configured threshold), the maximum bandwidth available for RSVP-TE is reduced by that amount. The algorithm uses three time parameters: T (collection interval), k (number of samples to smooth), and N = k * T (adjustment interval).

At each adjustment, the system calculates: New Maximum-Reservable-Bandwidth = Initial Maximum-Reservable-Bandwidth - (average SR traffic * optional multiplier M). The multiplier M (default 1.0, range 0 to 2) allows fine-tuning: values below 1 understate SR traffic, above 1 overstate it. This approach mirrors how auto-bandwidth works for RSVP-TE LSPs and allows dynamic adaptation as traffic patterns change.
sections.plainLanguage: Every hour, count how many new buses are on the road. If the count is significantly higher than last hour, reduce how many old buses we allow on the road. Use a fudge factor if needed.

sections.title: Security Risks
sections.content:
When the two protocols coexist, a compromised SR traffic stream could maliciously consume bandwidth and disrupt RSVP-TE LSPs. The solution mitigates this by allowing RSVP-TE traffic to preempt SR traffic based on priority if the available bandwidth becomes exhausted. However, there is a window of vulnerability: the dynamic measurement solution relies on sampling at intervals, so a sudden burst of malicious SR traffic could cause traffic drops before the system detects and reacts to it.

The RFC recommends using the base SR security framework to guard against SR traffic hijacking and denial of service attacks. Additionally, operators should be aware that this solution introduces a new trigger for RSVP-TE LSP preemption based on available bandwidth changes.
sections.plainLanguage: A bad actor could flood the new bus system to jam up the old system. The fix lets the old system kick new buses off if needed, but there's a brief window where trouble could happen. So watch the new system carefully.
